subtype: Approach: watching how others behave before joining in [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday night. Dear diary, this is my fourth day in Class 6 and I have said almost nothing. I'm Charu. It's not that I'm scared; I'm collecting information. The girls near the window sit together and talk about a singer. The boys play catch with a rolled-up sheet at recess, and Tanvir always stands near the door and is invited by everyone. Nobody sits at the back left. Someone new could go there. I have noticed who laughs at whose jokes, and I think the drawing club might be friendly. On Thursday I might ask Tanvir about it. Not yet. First I need to know who's who. 🙂

qa.q: Where does Tanvir usually stand at recess?
qa.a: Tanvir usually stands near the door.

qa.q: Why does Charu say the quiet days are not because of fear?
qa.a: Charu says the quiet days are about collecting information, which shows a calm and thoughtful mood and a plan to choose whom to approach.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Charu use if watching takes too long, and why?
qa.a: Charu could say hello to one person and ask about the drawing club. One short conversation gives new information faster than watching alone.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see the new girl who is quiet?
qa.a: Tanvir may not have noticed Charu yet, or may see a new classmate who is shy, so a small hello from Charu could start a friendship.

grounding: Charu watches quietly in Class 6, noticing where children sit and what they play, using the days to understand before choosing whom to approach.

subtype: Approach: introducing himself and asking someone to play [Action]
passage: Friday. I was so nervous I nearly did not go, but I told myself: just walk up. At lunch I found a group with a football, and I stood near them until there was a gap. "Hi, I'm Rehan. I just moved here from Kanpur. Can I play?" One boy, Vidya, grinned and said, "Sure, you're on my team!" Another asked about my old school, and I told him about the cricket ground behind it. By the end of lunch my knees were muddy and my heart was light. It was one small sentence, and it worked. I'll do it again on Monday with someone else.

qa.q: Where did Rehan say the move was from?
qa.a: Rehan said the move was from Kanpur.

qa.q: How did Rehan feel after the friendly answer?
qa.a: Rehan felt welcome and happy, shown by the light heart and the plan to try again on Monday. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rehan use if a group says no, and why?
qa.a: Rehan could try another group or ask the teacher who might like to play. A refusal is only one group's answer, and many others may say yes.

qa.q: How did Vidya's reply affect the new boy?
qa.a: Vidya grinned and put Rehan on the team straight away, so Rehan felt included at once and the nerves eased.

grounding: Rehan introduces the new arrival from Kanpur and asks to join a game, and the friendly response makes Rehan feel welcome.

subtype: Approach: staying alone and waiting for others to come [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Ira. When I started at the new school, I sat alone at lunch every day, holding my tiffin, hoping somebody would say 'Come and sit here.' Nobody did. I looked at the door and my tiffin in turn. Later I found out what the class thought: Bhupen told me they'd assumed I liked being alone, because I never looked up. But I looked up. I just never smiled. By Thursday my throat was tight and I ate only half my lunch. Each day was longer than the last. Waiting felt safe, because nobody could say no, but nothing changed either.

qa.q: What did Ira hold while sitting alone at lunch?
qa.a: Ira held a tiffin.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling by Thursday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ira felt lonely and sad; the tight throat and half-eaten lunch show it. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ira try, and why?
qa.a: Ira could smile and say hello to one classmate, or ask the teacher to pair Ira with a friendly buddy. A small step from Ira would give others a sign that company is wanted.

qa.q: How did the class see Ira?
qa.a: The class assumed that Ira liked being alone because Ira never seemed to look up, so they did not go over to Ira.

grounding: Ira sits alone hoping for an invitation, classmates assume it is a choice and stay away, and each day feels lonelier.

subtype: Approach: using a shared interest to start talking [Thinking]
passage: Wednesday. Diary, today was good! In art period I noticed Himani drawing a cricket player with a huge bat. I never talk first, but I thought: what do I really know? I know cricket. So I leaned over and said, "Is that a batsman? I love cricket! Who's your favourite?" She looked up, surprised, and said, "Everyone in blue!" We talked about the last match until the teacher told us to stop. Then Himani said, "Sit with us at lunch tomorrow." I felt my chest go warm. It was so easy when I started from something I already liked. I'm going to bring my own bat on Friday. Ojas.

qa.q: What was Himani drawing in art period?
qa.a: Himani was drawing a cricket player with a huge bat.

qa.q: What did Ojas think before speaking to Himani?
qa.a: Ojas thought about a known strength, cricket, and felt brave enough to start talking about it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ojas use with a classmate who does not like cricket, and why?
qa.a: Ojas could ask what the classmate enjoys doing and listen for a shared interest. Curiosity about the other person gives a starting point too.

qa.q: How might Himani have seen the talk?
qa.a: Himani looked up surprised and then invited Ojas to lunch, so Himani probably felt pleased that someone noticed the drawing and shared the interest.

grounding: Ojas notices a classmate drawing cricket players and says a love of cricket is shared, and the common interest gives an easy way to start talking.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher to pair him with a buddy [Action]
passage:
Monday. Vinay stood in the corridor of his new school, clutching his bag. He did not know where the canteen was, or the library, or even where to turn. At the end of the day he went to Leela Ma'am's desk. "I don't know where things are, ma'am."

Tuesday. Leela Ma'am smiled. "This is Vandana. She'll show you around." Vandana pointed out the canteen, the library and the water tank.

Friday. Vinay walked to the library alone and found the shelf he wanted. "Thanks, Vandana," he said at lunch. She shrugged, and pushed over her tiffin for him to share.

qa.q: Who showed Vinay around the school?
qa.a: Vandana showed Vinay around the school.

qa.q: What was Vinay feeling in the corridor on Monday?
qa.a: Vinay was probably lost and anxious, clutching his bag because he did not know where anything was.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vinay use, and why?
qa.a: Vinay could ask another classmate or check a school map, but a named buddy gives regular help and friendly company.

qa.q: How might Vandana see being asked to show Vinay around?
qa.a: Vandana pointed out the places and later shared her tiffin, so Vandana probably found it easy and friendly, and possibly gained a new friend.

grounding: A new student tells the teacher he does not know where things are, and the teacher pairs him with a classmate who shows him the canteen, library and water tank.

subtype: Approach: trying too hard to impress with bragging [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Shalini. On my first day at the new school I wanted everyone to like me, so I told them my old school had a swimming pool and a big playground, and this one was small. I said I had a tablet, a phone and a video game console at home. Manoj rolled his eyes. The others drifted off to the other side of the room. At lunch I sat with the bragging still in my mouth, like a bad taste. I thought: why is nobody coming? I could not see that talking about everything I had made others feel they had nothing to say.

qa.q: What did Shalini say the old school had?
qa.a: Shalini said the old school had a swimming pool and a big playground.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling at lunch, and what shows it?
qa.a: Shalini felt puzzled and lonely; the bad taste and the question about why nobody was coming show it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shalini try, and why?
qa.a: Shalini could ask classmates about themselves and listen. People warm to someone who is curious about them more than someone who compares schools.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Shalini's talk?
qa.a: Manoj rolled his eyes, so the boasting seems annoying and unwelcoming to Manoj, who moved away with the others.

grounding: To be accepted, Shalini says the old school was better and that many gadgets are owned, and the classmates find it annoying and keep away.

subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]
passage: Tushar, I remember a girl called Meena who joined my class when I was in Class 6. For a week she talked about how good her old school was and how many gadgets she had. Nobody sat near her. On the eighth day she looked around and noticed that whenever she began, the others went quiet. Something was not working. The next morning she said, "Rohan, what did you do on Sunday?" and listened to the whole answer. Then she asked Lata about her dog. By Friday, they had saved her a place on the bench. I'm Lokesh, and I learned from her that listening makes people come closer.

qa.q: How long did Meena talk about her old school before noticing anything?
qa.a: Meena talked for a week.

qa.q: What did Meena feel when she noticed the others going quiet?
qa.a: Meena felt puzzled and probably a bit sad, because she realised her way of talking was not working.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Meena, and why?
qa.a: Meena chose to ask questions and listen instead of boasting, and that made others feel interested in and included by her.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt when Meena asked about his Sunday?
qa.a: Rohan was probably surprised and pleased, since the new girl who used to boast now listened to his whole answer.

grounding: After a week of bragging without friends, the girl notices classmates go quiet, starts asking questions and listening, and is invited to sit with them.

subtype: Approach: learning the routines with a written list [Action]
passage: On the first morning at the school in Haifa, Yosef got lost twice between classes and arrived late with his face hot. That night he took a clean page of his diary and wrote a list: bell times down the left side, room numbers in the middle, teachers' names on the right. He drew a small map of the corridor with arrows. Next day he glanced at the page before every break. Vera looked over and asked, "Is that a map?" "It's my cheat sheet," he said. By Thursday he did not need to look at all. The worried knot in his stomach had loosened.

qa.q: What three things did Yosef list in his diary?
qa.a: Yosef listed bell times, room numbers and teachers' names.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling on the first morning, and how did the list change it?
qa.a: Yosef felt anxious and embarrassed after getting lost, and the list reduced the unknown so the knot in his stomach loosened. 🙂

qa.q: What alternative approach could Yosef use, and why?
qa.a: Yosef could ask a teacher for a class buddy or ask Vera to walk with him. A friendly guide gives company as well as directions.

qa.q: How might Vera see Yosef's cheat sheet?
qa.a: Vera asked whether it was a map and seemed curious, so Vera likely sees a smart way to cope with a new school.

grounding: A boy writes the bell times, room numbers and teachers' names in his diary, and reducing the unknown makes him less worried and stops him getting lost.

subtype: Approach: telling parents about a hard day [Revision]
passage: Pema dropped his bag on the floor and did not speak through dinner. His mother put down her spoon. "Something happened?" After a long silence, Pema said, "Nobody talked to me at school. Not one person." His mother did not rush to fix it. She sat closer. "That sounds lonely. Is there one classmate you would like to know better?" Pema thought. "Parveen shares my love of drawing." "Then how about inviting Parveen home on Saturday?" Pema nodded, slowly. It was small enough to do. On Saturday he set out two paper sheets and two sets of pencils on the table.

qa.q: What did Pema say about school at dinner?
qa.a: Pema said nobody talked to him at school.

qa.q: What did Pema feel when nobody talked to him at school?
qa.a: Pema felt lonely and left out, shown by the silence through dinner and dropping the bag.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pema try at school, and why?
qa.a: Pema could ask Parveen a question about drawing in class or ask the teacher to pair him with a buddy. Small hellos are less scary than a big invitation.

qa.q: How does Pema's mother respond, and how might it feel to Pema?
qa.a: Pema's mother listened, sat closer and did not rush to fix it, so Pema probably felt understood and able to take a small step.

grounding: Feeling left out, a child tells his mother that no one talked to him, and she suggests inviting one classmate home, which he takes as a small, doable step.

subtype: Approach: breaking the song or play into small parts [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Devika stared at the script for the school play. Eight pages of lines, and the show was in ten days. Her stomach flipped. Then she drew three lines with a pencil and cut the role into four scenes. "Just Scene One today." She learned it by evening.

Tuesday. Scene Two was learned, and she ticked the box on her chart.

Wednesday. Naveen, who played her brother, ran lines with her after school. "You know Scenes One to Three already!" Devika grinned. "One scene a day. Tomorrow is the last one." The script did not look so big now.

qa.q: How many scenes did Devika split her part into?
qa.a: Devika split her part into four scenes.

qa.q: What did Devika feel when she first stared at the script?
qa.a: Devika felt nervous and overwhelmed, with a flip in her stomach at eight pages in ten days.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Devika use if she forgets a scene, and why?
qa.a: Devika could record herself reading the lines and listen to it, or practise with a friend. Hearing the words again helps them stay.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Devika's progress?
qa.a: Naveen ran lines with Devika and was impressed that three scenes were already known, so Naveen probably feels reassured about the play.

grounding: A girl in a school play divides her part into four scenes and learns one each day, so the long script feels less scary and she can check her progress.
